en: The [treatise] on the five aggregates.
Homage to Mañjuśrī, the Youthful One!
The five aggregates are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
1. What is form? Whatever is form, all that consists of the four great elements and what is derived from the four great elements.
1.1 What are the four great elements? They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
1.1.1 In that regard, what is the earth element? It is solidity.
1.1.2 What is the water element? It is moisture. 1.1.3 What is the fire element? It is heat.

1.1.4 What is the wind element? It is lightness and mobility. 1.2 What is derived matter? It consists of the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, and the body faculty; as well as visible form, sound, odor, taste, a portion of the tangible, and non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
1.2.1 What is the eye faculty? It is the translucent matter whose object is visible form.
1.2.2 What is the ear faculty? It is the translucent matter whose object is sound. 1.2.3 What is the nose faculty? It is the translucent matter whose object is odor.
1.2.4 What is the tongue faculty (*jihvendriya*)? It is the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) whose object is taste.
1.2.5 What is the body faculty (*kāyendriya*)? It is the translucent matter whose object is the tangible.
1.2.6 What is visible form (*rūpa*)? It is the object of the eye—namely, color, shape, and informative intimation (*vijñapti*).
1.2.7 What is sound? It is the object of the ear; it has as its cause the great elements (mahābhūta) that are appropriated, unappropriated, or both.
1.2.8 What is odor? It is the object of the nose; it is pleasant odor, unpleasant odor, and that which is other than these.
1.2.9 What is taste? It is the object of the tongue; it consists of sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.

1.2.10 What is the portion of the tangible? It is the object of the body [faculty], excluding the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), consisting of smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, and thirst.
1.2.11 What is non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)? It is form (*rūpa*) born of informative action (*vijñapti*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is invisible and non-obstructive.

2. What is feeling (*vedanā*)? It is a threefold experience: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Pleasant [feeling] is that for the cessation of which there arises a desire for union; painful [feeling] is that from the arising of which there arises a desire for separation; neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] is that from the arising of which neither of those two [desires] occurs.
3. What is perception (*saṃjñā*)? It is the grasping of the signs of objects. It is of three kinds: limited, exalted, and immeasurable.
4. What are the formations? They are the mental factors other than feeling and perception, as well as the factors dissociated from thought.
4.1 What are the mental factors (caitasika-dharma)? They are those phenomena which are associated with the mind (citta).
Furthermore, what are they?

Contact, attention, feeling, perception, volition, desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, faith, shame, dread, the wholesome root of non-greed, the wholesome root of non-hatred, the wholesome root of non-delusion, vigor, serenity, heedfulness, equanimity, non-harming, attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, doubt, anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, guile, arrogance, harmfulness, lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, restlessness, lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, loss of mindfulness, distraction, lack of clear comprehension, regret, torpor, applied thought, and sustained thought.
Among these, five are universal, five have specific objects, eleven are wholesome, six are primary afflictions, and the remaining four are secondary afflictions that may also be otherwise.
4.1.1 What is contact (*sparśa*)? It is the discernment that arises from the coming together of the three. 4.1.2 What is attention (*manaskāra*)? It is the mental application of the mind.
4.1.5 What is volition (*cetanā*)? It is the mental formation of the mind—mental action—that proceeds by way of [perceiving] qualities, faults, or neither.
4.1.6 What is desire (*chanda*)? It is the longing for an intended object.

4.1.7 What is resolve (*adhimokṣa*)? It is the ascertainment of a determined object exactly as it is. 4.1.8 What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)? It is the non-forgetting of a familiar object and the mental state of recollecting it.
4.1.9 What is concentration (*samādhi*)? It is one-pointedness of mind upon the object under investigation.

4.1.10 What is wisdom (*prajñā*)? It is the discernment of that very same [object], whether it is correctly applied, incorrectly applied, or otherwise. 4.1.11 What is faith (*śraddhā*)? It is conviction regarding the results of actions, the [Four] Truths, and the [Three] Jewels, as well as clarity of the mind.

4.1.12 What is *hrī*? It is shame regarding a fault, having made oneself or the Dharma the dominant influence. 4.1.13 What is *apatrāpya*? It is shame regarding a fault, having made the world the dominant influence.
4.1.14 What is non-greed (*alobha*)? It is the antidote to greed, characterized by disenchantment and non-grasping.

4.1.15 What is non-hatred? It is loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the antidote to hatred. 4.1.16 What is non-delusion? It is the antidote to delusion, which is correct comprehension of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-sampratipatti*).
4.1.17 What is vigor (*vīrya*)? It is the antidote to laziness (*kausīdya*), the mental enthusiasm for what is wholesome.
4.1.18 What is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*)? It is the antidote to rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*), consisting in the serviceability (*karmaṇyatā*) of body and mind.

4.1.19 What is heedfulness (*apramāda*)? It is the antidote to heedlessness (*pramāda*), consisting in non-attachment (*alobha*) up to diligence (*vīrya*). Relying upon these, one abandons unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*) and cultivates the wholesome states that are their antidotes. 4.1.20 What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)? It is that same [set of factors] from non-attachment up to diligence, relying upon which one attains evenness of mind, serenity of mind, and effortlessness of mind; by means of which, when afflicted states have been expelled, one dwells without affliction.
4.1.21 What is non-harming? It is compassion, the antidote to harming.
4.1.22 What is attachment? It is affection and clinging toward the five aggregates of grasping.
4.1.23 What is hostility? It is malice toward sentient beings.
4.1.24 What is pride (*māna*)? There are seven types of pride: pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, the pride of "I am," conceit, inferiority pride, and false pride.

4.1.24.1 What is pride? It is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I am superior to one who is inferior," or "I am equal to one who is my equal. 4.1.24.2 What is excessive pride (*atimāna*)? It is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I am superior to one who is my equal," or "I am equal to one who is superior."
4.1.24.3 What is conceit (*māna*) and overweening pride (*atimāna*)? It is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I am superior" toward one who is superior.
4.1.24.4 What is the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*)? It is that inflation of the mind of one who regards the five aggregates of clinging as self or as belonging to a self.
4.1.24.5 What is arrogance (*abhimāna*)? It is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I have attained it," regarding a higher, distinguished realization that has not yet been attained.

4.1.24.6 What is *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride)? It is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I am only slightly inferior" to one who is vastly superior. 4.1.24.7 What is *mithyāmāna* (false pride)? It is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I possess qualities," when one actually possesses no qualities.

4.1.25 What is *avidyā* (ignorance)? It is the lack of knowledge regarding the results of karma, the [Four] Truths, and the [Three] Jewels. Furthermore, it is both innate (*sahajā*) and conceptually constructed (*parikalpitā*). Desire belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*), aversion, and ignorance belonging to the realm of desire—these three are the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*): greed as an unwholesome root, hatred, and delusion.

4.1.26 What is view (*dṛṣṭi*)? There are five views: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). 4.1.26.1 What is the view of a self-identity? It is the afflicted wisdom (*kliṣṭā prajñā*) of one who regards the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as a self or as belonging to a self. 4.1.26.2 What is the view of grasping at extremes? It is the afflicted wisdom of one who, taking that very [view of a self-identity] as the basis, regards [the self] as either eternal (*śāśvata*) or subject to annihilation (*uccheda*).
4.1.26.3 What is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)? It is afflicted wisdom (*kliṣṭā prajñā*) that either denies the cause, the fruit, or the action, or destroys an existing reality.

4.1.26.4 What is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)? It is afflicted wisdom that regards those same three types of views, as well as the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) which serve as their basis, as being foremost, excellent, distinguished, and supreme.

4.1.26.5 What is adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)? It is the afflicted wisdom of one who regards morality, observances, and the five aggregates of clinging that serve as their basis, as being purity, liberation, and the means to deliverance.

4.1.27 What is doubt (*vicikitsā*)? It is indecision regarding the [Four] Truths and so forth. Among the afflictions, three views and the last [affliction, doubt] are exclusively imagined (*parikalpita*); the remaining [afflictions] are both innate (*sahaja*) and imagined. 4.1.28 What is anger (*krodha*)? It is a mental resentment arising from a present harm.
4.1.29 What is enmity (*upanāha*)? It is the persistence of resentment.
4.1.30 What is hypocrisy (*mrakṣa*)? It is the concealment of one's own faults. 4.1.31 What is spite (*pradāśa*)? It is the biting of harsh speech.
4.1.32 What is envy (*īrṣyā*)? It is resentment of the mind toward the excellence of others.

4.1.33 What is avarice (*mātsarya*)? It is a mental grasping that is opposed to giving. 4.1.34 What is deceit (*māyā*)? It is the presentation of things as they are not, by one who intends to deceive others.
4.1.35 What is deceit (*śāṭhya*)? It is the crookedness of the mind comprised of the means for concealing one's own faults.
4.1.36 What is arrogance (*mada*)? It is the elation of the mind and its total absorption in one who is attached to their own prosperity.
4.1.37 What is harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*)? It is the injuring of sentient beings.
4.1.38 What is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*)? It is the absence of shame regarding one's own faults.

4.1.39 What is lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*)? It is the absence of shame regarding one's faults in the presence of others. 4.1.40 What is lethargy (*styāna*)? It is the unserviceability and rigidity of the mind.

4.1.41 What is restlessness? It is the lack of tranquility of the mind. 4.1.42 What is lack of faith? It is the absence of conviction regarding karma, its results, the truths, and the jewels; it is the lack of clarity of the mind and is the opposite of faith. 4.1.43 What is laziness? It is the lack of enthusiasm of the mind toward the wholesome and is the opposite of vigor.

4.1.44 What is negligence (*pramāda*)? It is that by which, through passion, hatred, delusion, and laziness, one does not protect the mind from affliction and does not cultivate the wholesome. 4.1.45 What is loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*)? It is afflicted mindfulness, which is the failure to maintain the presence of what is wholesome. 4.1.46 What is distraction (*vikṣepa*)? It is the wandering of the mind toward the five strands of sensual pleasure, consisting of portions of passion, hatred, and delusion.

4.1.47 What is lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*)? It is wisdom associated with the afflictions that consists in dwelling without awareness regarding the activities of body, speech, and mind.
4.1.48 What is remorse (*kaukṛtya*)? It is the mental state of regret.
4.1.49 What is torpor (*middha*)? It is a contraction of the mind characterized by a lack of independent functioning.

4.1.50 What is *vitarka*? It is a mental discourse that investigates; it is a specific form of volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). It is the grossness of the mind. 4.1.51 What is *vicāra*? It is a mental discourse that examines, in the same manner [as *vitarka*]. It is the subtlety of the mind.

4.2 What are the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*)? They are those which are designated in relation to the states of form, mind, and mental factors, yet cannot be designated as being either identical to or different from them.

What, then, are they? They are: acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the state of non-perception (*āsañjñika*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneity of the group (*nikāya-sabhāgatā*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), impermanence (*anityatā*), the sets of names (*nāma-kāya*), the sets of phrases (*pada-kāya*), the sets of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), and the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). Such are the categories. 4.2.1 What is acquisition? It is obtaining (*pratilambha*) and possession (*samanvāgama*). Furthermore, it consists, as appropriate, of seeds (*bīja*), mastery (*vaśitā*), and manifestation (*sammukhībhāva*).

4.2.2 What is the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)? It is the cessation of unstable mental states and mental factors through a mental attention preceded by the perception of liberation, in one who is free from passion for the *śubhakṛtsna* [heaven] but not for what is above it.

4.2.3 What is the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)? It is the cessation of unstable mental states and mental factors, and of some stable ones, through a mental attention preceded by the perception of dwelling in peace, in one who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and has transcended the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

4.2.4 What is non-ideation (*āsañjñika*)? It is the fruit of the attainment of non-ideation (*asañjñi-samāpatti*); it is the cessation of unstable mental states and mental factors for one reborn among the gods who are non-ideational beings.

4.2.5 What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)? It is the determination of the duration of existence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within a particular class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), projected by prior karma.
4.2.6 What is homogeneity of class (*nikāyasabhāgatā*)? It is the similarity of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) among sentient beings.
4.2.7 What is birth (*jāti*)? It is the coming into being of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within a homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), having previously not existed.

4.2.8 What is aging (*jarā*)? It is the alteration of the continuity of those very same phenomena in that same manner. 4.2.9 What is duration (*sthiti*)? It is the persistence of the continuity of those very same phenomena in that same manner.

4.2.10 What is impermanence? It is the cessation of their continuity in that very same manner. 4.2.11 What are the sets of names (*nāmakāya*)? They are the designations for the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharma*).
4.2.12 What are the sets of phrases (*padakāya*)? They are the designations for the specific qualities of phenomena.

4.2.13 What are the sets of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*)? They are the syllables (*akṣara*), based on their function of manifesting both [names and phrases]. These are also the phonetic sounds (*varṇa*), based on their function of describing the meaning by serving as the basis for names and phrases. Furthermore, the nature of being a syllable (*akṣaratva*) is based on the fact that it is not subject to change (*akṣaraṇa*) through synonyms. 4.2.14 What is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)? It is the non-acquisition of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
This is called the aggregate of formations.

5. What is consciousness (*vijñāna*)? It is the representation of an object (*ālambana-vijñapti*). It is also called mind (*citta*) and intellect (*manas*), based on its variety and its being the support for the intellect (*manaḥ-sanniśrayatā*). Furthermore, it is primarily the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). For that mind contains the seeds of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Moreover, that consciousness has an indeterminate object and aspect; it is of a single nature and continues as a stream.

Because, for one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñisamāpatti*), or the state of non-perception (*āsañjñika*), the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*)—known as the representation of objects—arises again, depending upon the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), and by virtue of its functioning in various modes, its resuming after being interrupted, and its engagement with and withdrawal from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

Furthermore, the state of being the *ālayavijñāna* is based on its being the repository of all seeds, its being the cause for the repository of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), and its being dissolved within the body. The *ādānavijñāna* is also so called because it appropriates that body. Primarily, the *manas* has the *ālayavijñāna* as its object; it is a consciousness always associated with self-delusion, self-view, self-pride, self-love, and so forth, which is of a single nature and continues as a stream, except during the states of Arhatship, the Noble Path, and the attainment of cessation.

In what sense are they called "aggregates" (*skandha*)? In the sense of a "heap" (*rāśi*). This is because they comprise a concise collection of form and the other [factors], which are differentiated by distinctions of time, continuity, type, destiny, and location.

The twelve bases (āyatana): 1) the eye base, 2) the form base, 3) the ear base, 4) the sound base, 5) the nose base, 6) the odor base, 7) the tongue base, 8) the taste base, 9) the body base, 10) the tangible base, 11) the mind base, and 12) the mental-object base.
1–9 The exposition of the eye and so forth is as previously described; [the exposition] of the bases of visible form, sound, odor, and taste [is likewise].
10 The base of the tangible consists of the great elements and that portion of the tangible which has been mentioned.
11 The base of the mind is the aggregate of consciousness.
The sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) consists of feeling, perception, mental formations, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What is the unconditioned? It is space, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyānirodha*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*), and suchness (*tathatā*).
12.1.1 What is space? It is that which provides room for form.

12.1.2 What is cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyānirodha*)? It is a cessation that is not a dissociation (*visaṃyoga*). Furthermore, it is the absolute non-arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) without the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) to the afflictions (*kleśa*). 12.1.3 What is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*)? It is a cessation that is a dissociation. Furthermore, it is the absolute non-arising of the aggregates by means of the counteragent to the afflictions.
12.1.4 What is suchness? It is the true nature of phenomena, the selflessness of phenomena.
In what sense are they called "bases" (āyatana)? In the sense of being the gateways for the arising of consciousness.

The eighteen elements are: the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.

1. Herein, the elements of the eye and so forth, as well as the elements of visible form and so forth, are as they are established among the sense bases (*āyatana*). The six consciousness elements are cognitions (*vijñapti*) that rely upon the eye and so forth and have visible form and so forth as their objects. The mind element (*manodhātu*) consists of those very [consciousnesses] when they have immediately ceased. The establishment of the eighteen elements is for the purpose of illustrating the support of the sixth consciousness.

Thus, that which is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of ten bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), as well as a portion of the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*). That which is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) consists of the mind-base (*manaāyatana*) and the seven elements of consciousness (*cittadhātu*). As for the other three aggregates and the remaining portion of the aggregate of form, these constitute the base of mental objects and the element of mental objects, together with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). In what sense are they "elements" (*dhātu*)? In the sense of maintaining their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) without activity (*nirvyāpāra*).

For what purpose is the teaching of the aggregates and so forth? It is as an antidote to the three kinds of grasping at a self, respectively. The three kinds of grasping at a self are: grasping at oneness, grasping at being an enjoyer, and grasping at being an agent.

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are material? Those whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). How many are immaterial? The remainder. How many are visible? One: the element of visible form (*rūpadhātu*), by virtue of being visible in space. How many are invisible? The remainder. How many are resistant (*sapratigha*)? Ten material elements, insofar as they are that which resists or that wherein resistance occurs. How many are non-resistant? The remainder. How many are with-outflows (*sāsrava*)?

Fifteen [elements] and a portion of the last three [of the eighteen elements]. Among these, they are included because they are the objects of direct perception for the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*). How many are untainted (*anāsrava*)? A portion of the last three. How many are associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)? All of them. How many are associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)? Fourteen, excluding odor and taste, as well as the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses.

How many are associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyapratisaṃyukta*)? The last three which are contaminated (*sāsrava*). How many are non-associated (*apratisaṃyukta*)? Those same ones when they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). How many are included within the aggregates (*skandhasaṅgṛhīta*)? All except the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). How many are included within clinging (*upādānasaṅgṛhīta*)? Those which are contaminated. How many are wholesome (*kuśala*)? How many are unwholesome (*akuśala*)? How many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?

Ten are of three kinds: the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*), as well as the form, sound, and phenomena elements (*rūpa-, śabda-, dharma-dhātu*). Eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): the remaining ones. How many are internal? Twelve, excluding the form, sound, odor, taste, tangible, and phenomena elements. How many are external? The six that were excluded. How many have an object (*sālambana*)? The seven mind-elements and that portion of the phenomena element which consists of mental factors (*caitasika*).

How many are without an object? The remaining ten and a portion of the *dharmadhātu*. How many are with conceptualization (*savikalpa*)? The mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and a portion of the *dharmadhātu*. How many are without conceptualization (*avikalpaka*)? The remaining ones. How many are appropriated (*upātta*)? The five internal [elements] and a portion of four elements—namely, the elements of visible form, taste, odor, and the tangible. How many are non-appropriated (*anupātta*)? The remainder.

The remaining nine [elements] and a portion of the four [others] are [also included]. How many are "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*)? The five internal material [bases] are homogeneous by virtue of sharing the same nature as their respective consciousnesses. How many are "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*)? Those same [five] are partially homogeneous when devoid of their own consciousness, by virtue of sharing the same nature as their own class. Thus the five aggregates are completed. This is the work of the venerable master Vasubandhu.
